title: Genealogies
lead: The Bible's family lists trace God's promise through generations: from Adam to Noah and Abraham (Genesis 5; 11), the nations (Genesis 10), Judah to David (Ruth 4:18–22), the long lists of 1 Chronicles 1–9 and the returned exiles (Ezra 2), and in Matthew and Luke the line of Jesus. Ancient genealogies are often selective and arranged in patterns, and they include surprising people, such as Tamar, Rahab and Ruth.

sections.b: Genesis is organized by the formula "these are the generations of" (Genesis 2:4; 5:1; 6:9; 10:1; 11:10, 27; 25:12, 19; 36:1; 37:2). Lists of ten names, such as Adam to Noah and Shem to Abram, mark eras. Chronicles opens with nine chapters of names to show the returned exiles their place in Israel's story (1 Chronicles 1–9), and Ezra checks priestly descent by genealogy (Ezra 2:59–63). Matthew arranges Jesus' line in three groups of fourteen (Matthew 1:17), and Luke traces it back to Adam (Luke 3:23–38). Both skip or differ in places, which ancient readers did not find troubling: genealogies told who a person was, not always every link.
